before.quote:
Fix a dimension $d\ge1$, side lengths $L_j>0$, integers $N_j\ge2$, directional diffusivities $\kappa_j>0$, and spacings $h_j=L_j/N_j$. For a finite periodic rectangular grid let
$$
G_h^{\rm per}=\prod_{j=1}^d(\mathbb Z/N_j\mathbb Z),\qquad \langle v,w\rangle_h=\Bigl(\prod_{j=1}^d h_j\Bigr)\sum_{i\in G_h^{\rm per}}v_iw_i,
$$
and define the positive centered heat operator, with indices reduced modulo $N_j$, by
$$(A_h^{\rm per}v)_i=\sum_{j=1}^d\kappa_j\frac{2v_i-v_{i+e_j}-v_{i-e_j}}{h_j^2}.$$

For a two-dimensional Dirichlet rectangle, use the nodes and weighted interior inner product of [[def-rectangular-grid-and-dirichlet-flux-stencil]]. At an interior node $(i,j)$ define
$$(A_h^{B}V)_{ij}=\kappa_x\frac{2V_{ij}-V_{i+1,j}-V_{i-1,j}}{h_x^2}+\kappa_y\frac{2V_{ij}-V_{i,j+1}-V_{i,j-1}}{h_y^2},$$
where values on boundary neighbours are the prescribed Dirichlet row $B$. Write $A_h^0$ for the square matrix on interior values when the boundary is zero. For any boundary vector $B$, let $c_h(B)$ be the result of applying this stencil to the grid vector that equals $B$ on the boundary and $0$ at interior nodes. Then $A_h^B V=A_h^0V+c_h(B)$ on interior nodes.

Let $T>0$, an integer $M\ge1$, $\Delta t=T/M$, $t_n=n\Delta t$, and $\theta\in[0,1]$. Given interior initial data $U^0$, interior source samples $F^n$, and, in the Dirichlet case, boundary rows $B^n$ for $0\le n\le M$ whose time-zero row agrees with the initial grid data, the periodic update is
$$
\frac{U^{n+1}-U^n}{\Delta t}+A_h^{\rm per}\bigl((1-\theta)U^n+\theta U^{n+1}\bigr)=(1-\theta)F^n+\theta F^{n+1},\quad 0\le n<M.
$$
The Dirichlet update, with the boundary values imposed at every time level, is
$$
\frac{U^{n+1}-U^n}{\Delta t}+A_h^0\bigl((1-\theta)U^n+\theta U^{n+1}\bigr)=(1-\theta)\bigl(F^n-c_h(B^n)\bigr)+\theta\bigl(F^{n+1}-c_h(B^{n+1})\bigr),\quad 0\le n<M.
$$
Thus the interior rows use the exact boundary contributions at both endpoints of the time step. The choices $\theta=0,1/2,1$ are forward Euler, Crank–Nicolson, and backward Euler applied to the spatially semidiscrete heat equation; this definition does not redefine those ODE time-stepping procedures.

For a homogeneous-source update with periodic rows or zero Dirichlet boundary values, let $Q_h$ be its one-step linear map when that step is well defined, and give it the operator norm induced by $\|\cdot\|_h$. The family is **grid-norm power stable on $[0,T]$** if there is $C_T<\infty$, independent of the grid and time step, such that $\|Q_h^n\|_{h\to h}\le C_T$ whenever $n\Delta t\le T$. This is a statement in the mesh-dependent finite grid norms defined above.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

$$\ker(\exp)=2\pi i\mathbb Z,$$
and $\exp z=\exp w$ exactly when $z-w\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(2x)=2\sin x\cos x,\quad \cos(2x)=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=2\cos^2x-1=1-2\sin^2x,$$
and
$$\sin^2x=(1-\cos2x)/2,\qquad \cos^2x=(1+\cos2x)/2.$$
When defined, $\tan(2x)=2\tan x/(1-\tan^2x)$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

Let $N\ge1$ and let $k,\ell\in\mathbb Z$. Then

$$\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N}=\begin{cases}N,&k\equiv\ell\pmod N,\\\\ 0,&k\not\equiv\ell\pmod N.\end{cases}$$

At $N=1$ the congruence holds for all $k,\ell$ and the sum is $1$. The sum is the finite sum of the complex family $x\mapsto e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N}$ over the von Neumann natural $N=\{0,\dots,N-1\}$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]), and $N$ on the right is the natural number $N$ read in $\mathbb C$ as the additive multiple $N\cdot1_{\mathbb C}$, that is, the value at $N$ of the canonical embedding $\mathbb N\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-integer-multiples-agree-with-canonical-natural]]).

Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid and let all index sets below be finite.

1. If $h:T\to S$ is a bijection and $a:S\to M$, then $\sum_{t\in T}a_{h(t)}=\sum_{s\in S}a_s$.
2. If $S$ and $T$ are disjoint and $a:S\cup T\to M$, then $\sum_{u\in S\cup T}a_u=\sum_{s\in S}a_s+\sum_{t\in T}a_t$.
3. If $a:S\times T\to M$, then
   $$\sum_{(s,t)\in S\times T}a_{s,t}=\sum_{s\in S}\left(\sum_{t\in T}a_{s,t}\right)=\sum_{t\in T}\left(\sum_{s\in S}a_{s,t}\right).$$

Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$

$$f(x)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},$$

the right-hand side being independent of the chosen integer representative of the class $x$. Consequently $\mathcal F_N$ is bijective with inverse the positive-sign transform

$$(\mathcal G_Ng)(x):=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}g(k)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},\qquad g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N},\ x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z,$$

and there is no convergence, regularity or support hypothesis anywhere.

operations.before: For each coordinate $j$, the mode satisfies $\phi_\ell(i+e_j)=e^{2\pi\mathrm i\ell_j/N_j}\phi_\ell(i)$ and $\phi_\ell(i-e_j)=e^{-2\pi\mathrm i\ell_j/N_j}\phi_\ell(i)$. Substitution into the $j$th stencil term gives $\kappa_jh_j^{-2}(2-e^{2\pi\mathrm i\ell_j/N_j}-e^{-2\pi\mathrm i\ell_j/N_j})\phi_\ell(i)=4\kappa_jh_j^{-2}\sin^2(\pi\ell_j/N_j)\phi_\ell(i)$. Summing over $j$ yields the asserted eigenvalue.
operations.after: Changing a representative $i_j$ by $N_j$ changes the exponent by the integer multiple $2\pi\mathrm i\ell_j$, so [F2] makes $\phi_\ell$ well-defined on the periodic grid. It is nonzero because $\phi_\ell(0)=1$. Put $\beta_j=2\pi\ell_j/N_j$. The addition law gives $\phi_\ell(i\pm e_j)=e^{\pm\mathrm i\beta_j}\phi_\ell(i)$, including wrapped indices. By [F2], $e^{\mathrm i\beta_j}$ has modulus one and $e^{\mathrm i\beta_j}e^{-\mathrm i\beta_j}=1$, hence $e^{-\mathrm i\beta_j}=\overline{e^{\mathrm i\beta_j}}$. The Cartesian Euler formula in [F2] and [F3] therefore give $2-e^{\mathrm i\beta_j}-e^{-\mathrm i\beta_j}=2-2\cos\beta_j=4\sin^2(\beta_j/2)$. Substitution into [F1] yields the asserted eigenvalue on summing over $j$; it is nonnegative because each $\kappa_j/h_j^2$ is positive and each sine square is nonnegative.

operations.before: For one coordinate, the finite geometric sum $\sum_{r=0}^{N_j-1}e^{2\pi\mathrm i qr/N_j}$ equals $N_j$ if $q$ is divisible by $N_j$ and equals $0$ otherwise. Therefore distinct modes are orthogonal in the complexified grid inner product. There are exactly $\prod_jN_j$ such nonzero modes, equal to the dimension of the grid space, so they form a basis.
operations.after: Put $P=\prod_{j=1}^dN_j>0$. By [F2], [F4] and the finite Fubini rule [F5], $\sum_{i\in G_h^{\rm per}}\phi_\ell(i)\overline{\phi_m(i)}=\prod_{j=1}^d\sum_{r=0}^{N_j-1}\exp(2\pi\mathrm i(\ell_j-m_j)r/N_j)$. This is $P$ when $\ell=m$ and zero otherwise: distinct index tuples have a coordinate whose two standard representatives are not congruent modulo $N_j$. Thus the nonzero modes are orthogonal, also after multiplying the pairing by the positive grid weight $\prod_jh_j$. Apply the published one-dimensional inversion formula [F6] successively to each of the $d$ coordinates of any grid vector. All sums are finite, so [F5] combines these expansions into a linear combination of the displayed product modes $\phi_\ell$; hence they span the complexified grid space. If a linear combination of them is zero, multiply it by $\overline{\phi_m}$ and sum over the grid. The displayed pairing identity leaves $P$ times its $m$th coefficient, so every coefficient is zero. The modes therefore form a basis.

operations.before: Let $M$ be the maximum of the cellwise suprema of $|\nabla v|$. Across every interior facet the polynomial traces agree; on every boundary facet they agree with zero. For a point $x$ in the mesh skeleton, its minimal mesh face is the unique mesh face whose relative interior contains $x$; the local star of that face means the union of the cells containing it. The incident simplicial cones in this star cut a small sphere about the face into a finite face-to-face triangulation of the local directions in $\Omega$. Within each connected component, top-dimensional pieces are connected by facet adjacency: perturb a path in that open component to avoid the finite union of codimension-two faces. At an interior point the direction set is the whole connected sphere, so matching traces make all incident polynomial values agree. At a boundary point every component has a boundary direction; following facet adjacencies reaches a boundary facet, where the polynomial value is zero, so all cell limits in that component are zero. Thus the cellwise continuous representatives and the exterior zero fit continuously on the whole finite polyhedral partition. Restrict this continuous function to any line segment. The segment is divided by the finitely many cell facets into finitely many intervals; on each cell interval its derivative along the segment has magnitude at most $M$, and on exterior intervals it is zero. Continuity at the interval endpoints then gives $|\widetilde v(x)-\widetilde v(y)|\le M|x-y|$ for all $x,y$. Thus $|v(x)|\le M\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^d\setminus\Omega)$.
operations.after: Let $M$ be the maximum of the cellwise suprema of $|\nabla v|$. Across every interior facet the polynomial traces agree; on every boundary facet they agree with zero. For a point $x$ in the mesh skeleton, its minimal mesh face is the unique mesh face whose relative interior contains $x$; the local star of that face means the union of the cells containing it. If the minimal face is a facet, there are exactly two incident cells at an interior facet and exactly one at a boundary facet. In the interior case their values at $x$ agree by the matching polynomial traces; in the boundary case the single cell value agrees with exterior zero by the zero boundary trace. For the remaining faces, let $c\ge2$ be their codimension. The incident simplicial cones in their local star cut a small sphere in the normal space of the face, of dimension $c-1$, into a finite face-to-face triangulation of the local directions in $\Omega$. Within each connected component, top-dimensional pieces are connected by facet adjacency: perturb a path in that open component to avoid the finite union of codimension-two faces. At an interior point the direction set is the whole sphere, which is connected because $c\ge2$, so matching traces make all incident polynomial values agree. At a boundary point every component has a boundary direction; following facet adjacencies reaches a boundary facet, where the polynomial value is zero, so all cell limits in that component are zero. Thus in all cases the cellwise continuous representatives and the exterior zero fit continuously on the whole finite polyhedral partition. Restrict this continuous function to any line segment. The segment is divided by the finitely many cell facets into finitely many intervals; on each cell interval its derivative along the segment has magnitude at most $M$, and on exterior intervals it is zero. Continuity at the interval endpoints then gives $|\widetilde v(x)-\widetilde v(y)|\le M|x-y|$ for all $x,y$. Thus $|v(x)|\le M\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^d\setminus\Omega)$.
